name: Burg Kronburg
kurzbeschreibung: Burgruine Kronburg perches on a steep rocky crest above Zams: medieval cliffside fortress from c. 1380, Maria Hilf pilgrimage church, and convent estate.
beschreibung:
Overview

The history-steeped Burg Kronburg (also known as Ruine Kronburg) sits perched atop a striking, steeply rising rock cone at 1,066 metres above sea level, high above the Inn valley between the municipalities of Zams and Sch?nwies in the holiday region TirolWest. Surrounded by dense mountain forests and rugged precipices, the dramatically elevated ruin, together with the pilgrimage church of Maria Hilf nestled below, the historic inn, and the Klostergut Kronburg convent estate, forms a unique spiritual and cultural ensemble in the Tyrolean Oberland.

History & Pilgrimage

Archaeological discoveries suggest that the prominent castle hill was already utilised as a refuge in prehistoric times. The actual fortifications were constructed around 1380 by the nobleman Johann von Starkenberg to maintain military control over the Inn valley. Following the unsuccessful Starkenberg feud against Tyrolean sovereign Friedrich IV. mit der leeren Tasche, the castle was besieged in 1423 and fell to the provincial princes. In 1504, Emperor Maximilian I. bestowed the Kronburg upon the influential Fieger noble family, who transformed it into a comfortable residence. After the complex fell into disuse in the latter half of the 18th century and the dynasty became extinct in 1802, the fortress gradually fell into ruin. In 1985, the 'Rettet die Kronburg' association rescued the masonry through comprehensive restoration work. On the saddle beneath the castle rock, the pilgrimage site of Maria Hilf emerged from 1673 onwards following miraculous healings; the Baroque pilgrimage church was expanded between 1714 and 1717. Today, the monastery estate is lovingly managed by the Barmherzige Schwestern von Zams.

Visit & Getting There

The castle ruin Burgruine Kronburg is open year-round during daylight hours and freely accessible free of charge (entry at your own risk). The pilgrimage church Maria Hilf is also open during the day for prayer and visits; the adjacent Gasthof Kronburg tavern welcomes visitors during its seasonal opening hours. Getting there by public transport: by train to Landeck-Zams station, then by regional buses to Zams or Sch?nwies. Well-marked hiking paths (such as the Starkenberger Panoramaweg) lead from valley bus stops up to the monastery estate in about 45 to 60 minutes. By car: from the Inntalautobahn A12 or the B171 at Zams, follow the signs towards Kronburg; a paved mountain road leads directly to the visitor car park at Klostergut Kronburg. From the car park, a steep forest and rock trail leads up to the castle ruin in roughly 15 minutes.

Tips

The climb from the monastery estate to the castle ruins along the rocky path requires surefootedness and sturdy mountain boots; the trail to the ruins is not suitable for wheelchairs or strollers. In contrast, the grounds of the convent estate including the pilgrimage church and the inn are level and easily accessible. Kronburg is a popular stopping point along the Tyrolean Camino de Santiago (Tiroler Jakobsweg) ? pause to absorb the profound tranquility of the pilgrimage site and the magnificent view across the Landeck basin.
